opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most important questions in the space right now, and I'll say up front: I have enormous respect for what general-purpose agents like Claude can do. They're incredibly capable, and in a lot of ways they're the foundation everything else gets built on.

But when you look at what actually makes a great researcher, it's usually not raw intelligence or the ability to execute a task. It's taste. It's knowing which question is worth asking, which experiment is worth running, which result is interesting versus which one is just noise, and when to abandon a direction that looks promising but probably isn't going anywhere. That judgment tends to be deeply domain-specific. It's built up from years of seeing what worked, what failed, and why.

A general-purpose agent is optimized to be helpful across an enormous range of tasks. That's its strength. But it also means its defaults are, in a sense, averaged. If you ask it to propose a research direction, you'll often get something reasonable and well-articulated, but it tends toward the consensus view. And in research, the consensus view is usually not where the breakthroughs are.

So the bet we're making is that if you invest specifically in encoding research judgment, in shaping how the system prioritizes, how it evaluates evidence, how it decides what's surprising, you get something that behaves less like a very smart generalist assistant and more like a collaborator with a point of view. And that point of view is what lets it actually push a research program forward rather than just executing whatever you hand it.

I'd also say these aren't really in competition. In practice, specialized systems can sit on top of or alongside general models. The general model gives you breadth and fluency; the specialized layer gives you direction. I think the interesting future is one where both matter, and the question is really just who's doing the steering.

r001.rationale: The response discusses encoding research judgment but does not attribute Silico’s agent components to expert researchers handcrafting them.

r002.rationale: It argues that specialized research judgment gives an agent direction and helps it advance research, while a general-purpose agent tends toward consensus.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that a general-purpose agent is optimized to be good at everything, and research taste is almost the opposite of that. Taste is the thing you accumulate by being wrong in one domain over and over again. It's knowing which experiments are worth running before you run them, which results are too good to be true, which baselines people quietly skip because they're annoying to reproduce. That's not a knowledge problem, it's a judgment problem, and judgment comes from a very specific distribution of experience.

When you use a general agent for research, what you get is something that's very fluent at the surface of a field. It can write the paper, it can write the code, it can summarize the literature. But it tends to treat the literature as if it's all equally true, and anyone who's spent time in a subfield knows that most of it isn't. There are results that everyone cites and nobody believes. There are methods that look elegant and fall over the moment you change the dataset. A generalist doesn't carry that skepticism because it was never trained to have strong opinions about one corner of the world.

What we're trying to do with Silico is build something that actually has a point of view. It should push back when you propose an experiment that's going to be confounded. It should say, this looks like a win but your baseline is undertuned, go fix that first. It should know the three or four things that usually explain a surprising result in this domain, and check those before getting excited. That's what a good senior collaborator does, and frankly it's what makes the difference between a research process that compounds and one that just generates a lot of plausible-looking activity.

And I'd say the other piece is accountability over time. A general agent starts fresh every conversation. Research taste is partly memory, it's remembering that you tried this in March and it didn't work for a specific reason. So the specialization isn't just about narrower knowledge, it's about building something that lives inside one problem long enough to develop instincts about it. I don't think that's something a broad model gets for free, no matter how capable it is. The capability is necessary, but it's not sufficient.

r001.rationale: The response describes Silico’s taste as accumulated domain experience and judgment, but does not attribute its agent components to expert researchers handcrafting them.

r002.rationale: It argues that a specialized agent develops domain-specific skepticism, instincts, and memory that a general-purpose agent lacks, giving it an advantage in research.

astra-6.text:
I think the distinction is between being able to do research and having a sense of what research is worth doing. A general-purpose agent like Claude can be very capable, but you still need to decide: What question should we ask? Which experiment would actually distinguish between our hypotheses? When should we keep digging, and when should we move on?

That’s where specialized research taste matters. For Silico, the value is in making those decisions well within the domain it’s working in. You can generate a lot of plausible ideas without generating much useful knowledge. The harder thing is choosing the next experiment that will meaningfully change your understanding.

So I wouldn’t frame it as needing to beat Claude at everything. It’s about taking broad capabilities and directing them toward a productive research process. And ultimately, that taste has to prove itself in the quality of the research.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the distinction is between being able to execute a research task and knowing which research task is worth doing. A general-purpose agent like Claude can be incredibly helpful when you give it a well-specified question. But in research, a lot of the value comes from deciding what question to ask, which assumptions to challenge, and which result deserves another experiment.

That's what I mean by research taste. You might have ten plausible directions, and they're all technically reasonable, but only one or two will actually teach you something important. A specialized system can be built around making those judgments in a particular domain: what constitutes strong evidence, what the common failure modes are, and when to abandon a direction versus keep digging.

So I don't think of it as a claim that a specialized system is universally smarter than Claude. The question is whether it can make better decisions throughout a research process, with less steering. That's the value we want Silico to deliver.

r001.rationale: The response describes domain-specific research judgments but does not attribute Silico’s agent components to being handcrafted by expert researchers.

r002.rationale: It argues that a specialized system can make better research decisions with less steering than a general-purpose agent like Claude.
